extraction.name: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering)
extraction.description: PIQA is a benchmark dataset for evaluating physical commonsense reasoning in natural language models. The task is multiple choice question answering: given a physical goal expressed in natural language and two possible solutions, a model must choose the most appropriate solution. The dataset focuses on everyday situations with a preference for atypical solutions, inspired by instructables.com. It contains over 16,000 training QA pairs, with 2K development and 3K test examples.
extraction.creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi
extraction.publisher: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence; Microsoft Research AI; Carnegie Mellon University; Paul G. Allen School for Computer Science and Engineering, University of Washington
extraction.citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., & Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was collected through crowdsourcing using Amazon Mechanical Turk. Annotators were provided prompts derived from instructables.com and asked to construct goal-solution pairs. They were asked to glance at instructables and use them as inspiration to articulate a physical goal, a valid solution, and a 'trick' (incorrect solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong due to subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics). Annotators were seeded with instructables from six categories (costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop), with two examples per instructable.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Prompts derived from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for everyday tasks from cooking to car repair.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The AFLite algorithm was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples from the data. 5,000 examples from the original dataset were used to fine-tune BERT-Large and compute embeddings of all remaining instances. AFLite uses an ensemble of linear classifiers trained on random subsets of the data to determine whether precomputed embeddings are strong indicators of the correct answer option, and discards instances whose feature representations are collectively highly indicative of the target label. Examples with low agreement during validation were removed.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators completed a qualification HIT identifying well-formed (goal, solution) pairs (>80% required to participate in main HIT). In the main HIT, annotators were shown an instructable and asked to produce: 1) a physical goal, 2) a valid solution, and 3) a trick (incorrect solution). Annotators could use simple linguistic tricks (negation, numerical changes) or swap key actions/items. A 'diff' button was provided to highlight where solutions differ. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. Users with low agreement were de-qualified.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Examples with low annotator agreement during validation were removed from the data. This sometimes removed correct examples that required expert-level domain knowledge (e.g., woodworking terminology) which the authors deemed should not fall under 'commonsense'. Human performance (94.9%) was calculated by majority vote on development data.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotators were paid an average of >15$/hr according to self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations. No further demographic information provided.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Spacy (for tokenization and POS tagging); GPT BPE tokenizer; BERT-Large (used with AFLite for artifact removal)
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors argue that learning about the world from language alone is limiting, and that knowledge should be learned from interaction with the world. The dataset aims to provide language tools that capture physical knowledge to speed up bootstrapping of robotic-language applications.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The authors discuss 'reporting bias' as a motivating concern—commonsense physical properties are rarely directly reported in text. When annotators were asked for unconstrained (task, tool) pairs, reporting bias swamped the dataset with prototypical solutions (kitchen/garage tools). To address this, instructables prompts were used to flatten the distribution of referenced objects.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Some development 'mistakes' actually required web-search to verify. Examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge were removed during validation. Dataset truncated at 150 tokens affecting 1% of data. The authors note that matching humans on the dataset by fine-tuning on large in-domain data is not the point—the goal is to show limitations of learning from language alone.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Validation, Testing. The dataset is designed as a benchmark for evaluating physical commonsense understanding in natural language models. Folds were automatically produced by AFLite: training (16K+ QA pairs), development (2K), test (3K).
